messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi, a 53-year-old painter, had been working on a mural in a public square when a mortar shell struck a nearby market. The blast threw him off his ladder; he landed on his side, his body twisted, as smoke and dust filled the air. In the months that followed, the smell of burnt fabric or any sharp bang—a car backfiring, a door slamming—would send his heart racing and his muscles tensing, his body bracing for danger. To Ravi, each sharp bang or burning smell instantly confirmed that danger was everywhere, and he would think, “This is what the world is now.” Those same triggers would also drag him back into the memory: his limbs would lock into that same twisted position, and he would be overwhelmed by a wave of grief for the people he had seen injured. Each time, the memory felt so extreme that it seemed unreal, and he would think, “The world is a dangerous place—there is no safety anywhere.” These thoughts made him feel that nothing in his life mattered anymore, and that he was no longer capable of the work that had defined him.

Believing he was no longer the man he had been, Ravi began to avoid news reports about the conflict, certain that seeing them would only confirm his loss. He also started to keep himself busy at all hours, taking on extra painting jobs he did not need, because idleness brought the unbearable question of why this had happened to him. His conviction that the world was dangerous made him interpret every unfamiliar smell or sudden sound as a potential threat, scanning his environment for signs of trouble even in his own backyard. When he did remember the event, his negative appraisals colored the recollection: the grief felt even heavier because he believed he should have been able to help, and the unreal quality of the memory made him doubt his own mind.

The memory itself intruded without warning—his body would reenact the fall, and the accompanying grief would feel as fresh as the day it happened. In response, he would mentally go over the event again and again, searching for a reason why he had been singled out, and this rumination only made the memory more vivid and more frequent. Recalling the explosion also kept his body on high alert; he would lie in bed at night, tense and watchful, listening for sounds that might signal danger. Each intrusion reinforced his belief that he could no longer handle the ordinary demands of his life, deepening his sense of futility.

Living in a state of constant hypervigilance—his body always ready to react—Ravi found himself jumping at ordinary sounds like a neighbor closing a car door. The persistent sense of threat kept the explosion close in his mind, and the memory would surface without a trigger, as if the adrenaline itself called it up. This hypervigilance, in turn, made him more likely to notice potential triggers; a faint smell of smoke while cooking would immediately pull him into a memory of the blast. The threat he felt also drove him to keep busy, because slowing down meant confronting the fear that was always simmering beneath the surface. And his vigilance confirmed his appraisal that the world was dangerous: if he had to be this watchful, danger must be real.

Yet his efforts to manage only deepened the cycle. Keeping busy meant he spent long hours in his studio, where the smell of paint thinner—reminiscent of the dust and chemical odors from the blast—became an unavoidable trigger. Ruminating about why the event happened to him kept the memory alive, and avoiding the news left him unprepared for the occasional headline he could not escape, which would spike his anxiety. His constant busyness also left him exhausted, yet he could not stop, because stopping made him feel the tension in his body even more acutely.

Six months after the bombing, Ravi’s wife insisted he see a doctor. He came to the clinic not because he believed therapy could help, but because he was tired of living with a body that never relaxed and a mind that would not stop circling back to that single moment. What frightened him most was the thought that he might never feel capable again—that the man who had once painted with confidence was gone for good.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals cause or trigger the memory; it only shows that memory triggers appraisals or that appraisals color the memory after it occurs.
